title: Equivalent Expressions with Properties
trouble: Students multiply only the first term, writing 3(x + 2) = 3x + 2.

blocks.html: You used the distributive property to factor sums of numbers like $36 + 8 = 4(9 + 2)$. It works the same way with variables, and it lets you rewrite an expression without changing its value.
Equivalent expressions are equal for every value of the variable. The distributive property, $a(b + c) = ab + ac$, makes them: $3(x + 2) = 3x + 6$. So does combining like terms: $y + y + y = 3y$.

blocks.name: areamodel
blocks.cap: A 3 by $(x + 2)$ rectangle is a 3 by $x$ part and a 3 by 2 part: $3(x + 2) = 3x + 6$. Move the slider: the two areas stay equal for every $x$.

blocks.html: Picture a rectangle 3 units tall and $x + 2$ units long. Split it into a 3 by $x$ part (area $3x$) and a 3 by 2 part (area 6). The whole area is $3(x + 2)$; the parts add to $3x + 6$. Since it is the same rectangle, the two expressions are equal whatever length $x$ is. Combining like terms is the same property: $4a + 3a = (4 + 3)a = 7a$.

blocks.title: Expand
steps: The 3 multiplies each term inside: $3 \times x = 3x$ and $3 \times 2 = 6$.

blocks.title: Factor
steps: The greatest common factor of 12 and 18 is 6.

blocks.title: Combine like terms
steps: $4a$ and $3a$ are like terms: both count $a$’s.
$4a + 3a = 7a$. The 2 has no $a$, so it stays.

blocks.html: Multiplying only the first term: $3(x + 2) = 3x + 2$. Quick check: try $x = 1$. $3(1 + 2) = 9$, but $3(1) + 2 = 5$. They are not equal, so something was left out. The 3 must multiply the 2 as well.
